amaranth-wild-greens-patties.title: Amaranth and Wild Greens Patties
ingredients: 1 cup mixed wild greens (chickweed, sorrel, dandelion), finely chopped
instructions: Cook the amaranth: Cook the amaranth seeds in water until fully absorbed (15–20 min). Let cool slightly.
Mix: Combine cooked amaranth with greens, egg, flour, salt, and pepper.
Form: Shape small patties with wet hands.
Sauté: Cook in a pan with oil for 3–4 min per side until golden.
Serve: With yogurt sauce, pesto, or as a vegetarian burger alternative.

black-chanterelle-cream-sauce.title: Creamy Black Trumpet Sauce
ingredients: 100 g black trumpets (fresh or 30 g dried)
Salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: Prepare the mushrooms: If dried, soak in hot water for 20 min, then drain and squeeze.
Sauté aromatics: Melt butter in a pan, cook shallot and garlic until soft.
Add mushrooms: Add black trumpets and sauté 5–7 min.
Deglaze (optional): Add wine and reduce by half.
Add cream: Pour in cream, cook 5 min until slightly thickened. Adjust salt, pepper, thyme.
Serve: Perfect with fresh pasta, polenta, or roasted potatoes.

chanterelle-herb-tart.title: Chanterelle and Herb Tart
instructions: Clean the mushrooms: Clean chanterelles with a brush or damp cloth.
Sauté base: Heat oil in a pan, cook leek until soft. Add chanterelles and sauté for 5 minutes. Season with salt.
Prepare filling: Beat eggs with cream, herbs, salt, and pepper.
Assemble: Place puff pastry in a baking dish, add mushrooms and leeks, pour egg mixture on top.
Bake: Bake at 180°C for 25–30 minutes until golden.
Serve: Hot or cold, perfect for a woodland brunch.

chickweed-sorrel-salad-with-walnut-vinai.title: Chickweed and Sorrel Salad with Walnut Vinaigrette
ingredients: 1 small handful walnuts, toasted and chopped
instructions: Toast the walnuts: In a dry pan, toast walnuts for 3–4 minutes until fragrant. Let cool.
Wash the greens: Rinse chickweed and sorrel, then gently dry with a clean cloth.
Prepare vinaigrette: In a small bowl, whisk oil, vinegar, honey, salt, and pepper.
Toss the salad: In a large bowl, combine chickweed, sorrel, and walnuts. Dress with vinaigrette and toss gently.
Serve: Enjoy immediately as a fresh, slightly tangy salad.

chestnut-mushroom-soup.title: Chestnut and Mushroom Soup
ingredients: 150 g wild mushrooms (porcini or black trumpets ideal)
instructions: Sauté base: In a pot, melt butter and cook onion and garlic until soft.
Add mushrooms: Add chopped wild mushrooms and sauté for 5 minutes.
Add chestnuts and broth: Add chestnuts and pour in vegetable broth. Add thyme.
Cook: Bring to a boil, then lower heat and simmer for 20 minutes.
Blend: Remove thyme. Blend with an immersion blender until smooth.
Finish: Add cream if desired, adjust salt and pepper.
Serve hot, with rustic bread or a drizzle of truffle oil.

dandelion-flower-syrup.title: Dandelion Flower Syrup
instructions: Clean petals: Separate yellow petals from green parts (which are bitter). Rinse gently.
Prepare infusion: In a pot, bring water to a boil, add petals and simmer for 10 minutes.
Steep: Remove from heat and let infuse covered overnight.
Strain: Strain the liquid and discard petals. Add lemon juice and sugar to the liquid.
Cook: Simmer over low heat until it thickens into a syrup (20–30 minutes).
Store: Pour into sterilized jars. Great on pancakes, cheese, or in tea.

nettle-soup.title: Nettle Soup
ingredients: 2 large handfuls fresh nettle leaves (use gloves!)
instructions: Sauté aromatics: In a pot, heat butter and sauté onion and garlic until soft.
Add potatoes: Add potatoes and cook for 5 minutes.
Add broth: Pour in vegetable broth and bring to a boil.
Add nettles: After 10 minutes, add nettles and simmer for another 5–7 minutes.
Blend: Blend the soup with an immersion blender until smooth.
Finish: Add cream or oat milk if desired. Adjust salt and pepper.
Serve hot, with a drizzle of oil or croutons.

parasol-mushroom-schnitzel.title: Parasol Mushroom Schnitzel
instructions: Clean the mushrooms: Wipe the caps with a damp cloth. Do not wash under water.
Prepare the coating: Beat the egg in a bowl. In another, mix breadcrumbs, salt, pepper, and Parmesan.
Bread: Dip each cap in egg, then in the breadcrumb mixture.
Fry: Heat oil or butter in a pan. Fry the caps over medium heat until golden and crispy (about 3 minutes per side).
Serve: With lemon wedges and fresh salad. A vegetarian classic.

masterwort-infused-honey-glaze.title: Masterwort Root Honey Glaze
ingredients: 1 teaspoon dried masterwort root or 2 teaspoons fresh, grated
instructions: Warm the honey: In a small saucepan, gently heat honey and water over low heat.
Infuse: Add masterwort and lemon zest. Stir and keep on very low heat for 5–10 minutes (do not boil).
Strain: Remove from heat and strain through a fine sieve or cheesecloth.
Bottle: Pour into a clean jar.
Use: Perfect on roasted vegetables, grilled fruit, or game. Keeps in the fridge for weeks.

Cook the potatoes: In a pan, sauté potatoes and onion in olive oil until golden.

Add eggs: Beat eggs with salt and pepper, pour into the pan.

2 tablespoons grated cheese (e.g. Pecorino or Parmesan)

ingredients: 2–3 wild artichoke hearts, cleaned and sliced
Wild mint or fresh parsley to garnish
instructions: Prepare the artichokes: Remove outer leaves and choke. Thinly slice the hearts.
Sauté: Gently cook garlic and artichokes in oil for 10 minutes until tender.
Cook the pasta: Boil pasta in salted water until al dente. Reserve ½ cup cooking water.
Toss: Mix pasta with artichokes, lemon juice and zest, and the cooking water.
Serve: Add salt, pepper, and garnish with fresh herbs. Fresh, wild, Mediterranean.

lions-mane-crab-cakes.title: Lion's Mane "Crab" Cakes
ingredients: 300 g lion's mane, torn into shreds
1 teaspoon sweet paprika or seafood seasoning
Zest and juice of half a lemon
instructions: Dry-fry: Cook the shredded mushroom in a dry pan over medium heat, pressing it down, until it has given up its water and starts to brown (8–10 minutes). Let it cool.
Mix: Stir the egg, mayonnaise, mustard, paprika, spring onion, lemon zest and juice together, then fold in the mushroom and 4 tablespoons of breadcrumbs. Season.
Shape: Form 6 small cakes and coat them in the remaining breadcrumbs. Chill for 15 minutes so they hold together.
Fry: Fry the cakes in oil or butter over medium heat until golden and crisp, about 3–4 minutes per side.
Serve: With lemon wedges and a green salad or tartare sauce.

crispy-roasted-hen-of-the-woods.title: Crispy Roasted Hen of the Woods
ingredients: 400 g hen of the woods, torn into small clusters
instructions: Clean: Brush the soil and grit out from between the fronds and trim the tough core at the base. Do not soak it.
Season: Toss the clusters with the olive oil, soy sauce, garlic and thyme, and add pepper. The soy sauce brings the salt.
Roast: Spread them on a baking tray in a single layer and roast at 220 °C for 20–25 minutes, turning once, until the edges are brown and crisp.
Serve: Hot, with lemon wedges, over rice, polenta or toast.

grilled-saffron-milk-caps.title: Grilled Saffron Milk Caps with Garlic and Parsley
ingredients: 500 g young, firm saffron milk caps
A small bunch of flat-leaf parsley, finely chopped
instructions: Clean: Cut the stems off level with the caps and brush away pine needles and soil. Wipe the caps with a damp cloth rather than washing them.
Mix: Stir the garlic and parsley into 4 tablespoons of the olive oil with a pinch of salt.

Grill: Heat a griddle pan, plancha or barbecue until very hot. Brush the caps with the remaining oil and lay them gill-side up. Cook for 5–6 minutes without turning, until they soften and the cups fill with juice.
Finish: Spoon the garlic and parsley oil into the gills, grind over some pepper and cook for 1 more minute.
Serve: Straight away, sprinkled with flaky salt, with bread to mop up the juices.

safetyNotes: Before cooking, cut a cap or stem: a saffron milk cap bleeds carrot-orange to red milk. White or yellow milk means another milk cap. The woolly milk cap (Lactarius torminosus: a pinkish cap with a woolly, rolled-in edge and white milk) and similar white-milk species cause severe stomach upsets.
Saffron milk caps bruise green where handled, and they can turn your urine reddish after the meal. Both are harmless.

saffron-milk-cap-potato-stew.title: Saffron Milk Cap and Potato Stew
ingredients: About 500 ml hot water or vegetable stock
Salt and a little chopped parsley
instructions: Prepare: Brush the mushrooms clean, trim the stems and cut them into large pieces. Peel the potatoes, then cut partway into each one and snap off chunks: the rough edges release starch that thickens the stew.
Soften: Cook the onion gently in the olive oil for 8–10 minutes until soft. Add the garlic and cook for 1 minute more.

Add the mushrooms: Turn up the heat, add the saffron milk caps and cook for 5 minutes, until they release their juice. Take the pan off the heat and stir in the paprika (it burns easily), then put it back on the heat, pour in the wine and let it bubble for 2 minutes.

Simmer: Add the potatoes, the bay leaf and enough hot water or stock to barely cover. Season with salt and simmer, partly covered, for 20–25 minutes, until the potatoes are tender and the broth has thickened.
Serve: Let it rest for 5 minutes, sprinkle with parsley and serve with bread.

hedgehog-mushroom-risotto.title: Hedgehog Mushroom Risotto
instructions: Clean: Brush the caps and rub the spines underneath with your fingers to shake out needles and soil. On large, older mushrooms, scrape the spines off with a knife, as they can taste bitter. Cut into bite-sized pieces.
Brown: Fry the mushrooms in the olive oil over high heat for 6–8 minutes, without crowding the pan, until golden. Add the thyme leaves, season and set aside.
Toast: In a wide pan, soften the onion in half the butter, add the rice and stir for 2 minutes, until the grains turn translucent at the edges. Pour in the wine and let it evaporate.

Cook: Add the hot stock a ladle at a time, stirring often and letting each ladle be absorbed before the next, for about 18 minutes, until the rice is creamy but still firm to the bite. Stir in the mushrooms for the last 5 minutes.
Finish: Off the heat, beat in the rest of the butter and the Parmesan. Cover, rest for 2 minutes and serve with a few thyme leaves on top.

shaggy-mane-soup.title: Cream of Shaggy Mane Soup
ingredients: 500 g young shaggy manes, picked the same day
A small bunch of chives, chopped
instructions: Sort: Cook them within a few hours of picking. Use only firm, young caps that are white all the way up the gills: pink or black edges mean they are turning to ink. Trim the stem bases, wipe off any soil and slice them.
Soften: Melt the butter in a pot and cook the onion gently for 5 minutes. Add the potato and the mushrooms and cook, stirring, for 5 minutes, until the mushrooms collapse.
Simmer: Pour in the stock, season and simmer for 15 minutes, until the potato is soft.
Blend: Blend until smooth, stir in the cream and the lemon juice, and heat through without boiling. Adjust the salt and pepper.
Serve: Hot, sprinkled with chives, with toasted bread. Drink water or juice with it, not wine or beer.

safetyNotes: Cook shaggy manes within a few hours of picking: they digest themselves into black ink. Only use young ones that are still white all through the gills.

Its look-alike, the common ink cap (Coprinopsis atramentaria: grey, smooth, with no shaggy scales), causes a violent reaction with alcohol drunk in the hours before the meal or up to three days after it. So this soup is made and served without alcohol: if there is any doubt about what you picked, don't drink with it.
Don't pick shaggy manes from roadsides or polluted ground: they accumulate heavy metals.

giant-puffball-parmigiana.title: Giant Puffball Parmigiana
ingredients: 1 young giant puffball (about 600 g), pure white inside
instructions: Check: Cut the puffball in half from top to bottom and make sure it is pure white, firm and even all the way through. Peel off the outer skin and cut the flesh into 1 cm slices.
Sauce: Warm the garlic in 2 tablespoons of olive oil, add the passata and a few basil leaves, season and simmer for 15 minutes.
Fry: Dust the slices with flour and fry them in batches in a shallow layer of hot oil, 2–3 minutes per side, until golden. Drain on kitchen paper and salt lightly.
Layer: Spread a little sauce in a baking dish, then layer puffball slices, sauce, mozzarella, basil and Parmesan. Repeat, finishing with sauce, mozzarella and Parmesan.
Bake: Bake at 200 °C for 25 minutes, until bubbling and browned. Let it rest for 10 minutes before cutting.

warnings: Do not consume wild mushrooms unless identified by an expert.
safetyNotes: Always cut every puffball in half from top to bottom. If you see the outline of a cap, gills or a stem inside, it is a young Amanita still in its 'egg', which can be deadly.

Only eat it while the flesh is pure white, firm and even all the way through, like fresh mozzarella. Yellow, olive, brown or purple flesh means it is spoiling, or that it is an earthball (Scleroderma), which is poisonous and dark purple-black inside.
Giant puffball must always be cooked.

matsutake-rice.title: Matsutake Rice (Matsutake Gohan)
ingredients: 300 g Japanese short-grain rice (2 rice-cooker cups)
A few sprigs of mitsuba or chives to serve
instructions: Rinse: Wash the rice in cold water, changing it until it runs almost clear. Soak it in fresh water for 30 minutes, then drain well.
Clean: Don't wash the matsutake. Scrape the soil off the base of the stem with a knife, wipe the caps with a damp cloth and slice them lengthwise, about 3 mm thick.
Season: Put the rice in a heavy pot or rice cooker with the soy sauce, mirin, sake and salt, pour in the dashi and stir once. Lay the matsutake on top without stirring them in.
Cook: Cover, bring to the boil, then cook on the lowest heat for 13 minutes (or use the rice cooker's normal setting). Turn off the heat and leave it to steam, lid on, for 10 minutes.
Serve: Gently fold the matsutake through the rice and serve in bowls, topped with mitsuba or chives.

safetyNotes: In North America's Pacific Northwest, matsutake has a deadly look-alike, Amanita smithiana: white, with a swollen stem base that tapers into the soil like a root and is ringed with white scraps of veil, and without the spicy cinnamon smell. It destroys the kidneys, so check the base and the smell of every mushroom.
Pick matsutake without raking the ground or disturbing the soil: raking destroys the mycelium, and it is banned in many US national forests, where you also need a permit to pick.

pickled-ramps.title: Appalachian Pickled Ramps
ingredients: About 200 g ramps with their bulbs (40 or so), bought or gathered a few from each large patch
instructions: Clean: Cut off the roots and slip the loose outer skin off each bulb. Cut the leaves off where they meet the stem and keep them for another use, such as pesto or scrambled eggs. Wash the bulbs and stems well in cold water.
Pack: Stand the bulbs and stems upright in a clean, sterilised jar of about 400 ml, trimming them to fit.
Brine: Bring the vinegar, water, sugar, salt, mustard seeds, peppercorns, bay leaf and chilli to the boil, stirring until the sugar and salt dissolve.
Fill: Pour the hot brine over the ramps until they are covered by 1 cm, tucking the bay leaf down the side. Tap the jar to release any air bubbles and close it.
Mature: Leave to cool, then keep in the fridge. Wait at least 3 days before eating; they keep for up to 2 months in the fridge. Serve with soup beans and cornbread, in sandwiches or with cheese.

safetyNotes: Harvest sustainably. Ramps grow slowly, taking years from seed to harvest, and over-harvesting has wiped out whole patches. Take one leaf per plant and leave the bulb, or at most a few bulbs from a large, dense patch. Never clear a patch.
Picking is banned in some parks, including Great Smoky Mountains National Park. Quebec bans selling wild ramps and limits personal harvest to 200 g, or 50 bulbs or plants, per person per year.

Look-alikes are poisonous: lily of the valley, and false hellebore (Veratrum viride). Crush a leaf of every plant: ramps smell strongly of onion or garlic, and the look-alikes don't. The smell lingers on your fingers, so don't trust it once your hands already smell.

sauteed-fiddleheads.title: Sautéed Fiddleheads with Garlic and Lemon
ingredients: Grated zest of ½ lemon and 1 tablespoon lemon juice
instructions: Clean: Trim the brown ends of the stems. Rub off the brown papery scales with your fingers, then wash the fiddleheads in several changes of cold water, until the water stays clear.
Boil: Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil, add the fiddleheads and boil them for 15 minutes (or steam them for 10–12 minutes). Drain them and throw the cooking water away.
Sauté: Heat the butter and oil in a wide frying pan, add the garlic and cook gently for 1 minute. Add the fiddleheads and sauté over a medium-high heat for 3–4 minutes, until lightly browned.
Season: Take the pan off the heat, add the lemon zest and juice, and season with salt and pepper.
Serve: Straight away, as a side with fish or eggs, or piled on buttered toast.

Boil: Bring a large pan of salted water to the boil, add the fiddleheads and boil them for 15 minutes (or steam them for 10–12 minutes). Drain them and throw the cooking water away.
Sauté: Heat the butter and oil in a wide frying pan, add the garlic and cook gently for 1 minute. Add the fiddleheads and sauté over a medium-high heat for 3–4 minutes, until lightly browned.
Season: Take the pan off the heat, add the lemon zest and juice, and season with salt and pepper.
Serve: Straight away, as a side with fish or eggs, or piled on buttered toast.

safetyNotes: Pick only the ostrich fern. Its fiddleheads are smooth and bright green, with brown papery scales, and a deep U-shaped groove runs along the inside of the stem. Never pick bracken, which is fuzzy, has a branched top and is carcinogenic.

Never eat fiddleheads raw or undercooked: they have caused outbreaks of food poisoning. Wash them, then boil them for 15 minutes (or steam for 10–12 minutes) and throw the water away, before sautéing.
Pick no more than half of the fiddleheads from one crown, so the plant survives. In Germany the ostrich fern is protected, and picking it in the wild is forbidden.

cloudberry-cream.title: Norwegian Cloudberry Cream (Multekrem)
ingredients: 300 g ripe cloudberries, fresh or frozen and thawed
2 tablespoons caster sugar, for the berries
1 tablespoon icing sugar, for the cream
1 teaspoon vanilla sugar, or a few drops of vanilla extract
Krumkake cones or crisp almond biscuits to serve (optional)
instructions: Sweeten: Pick over the berries and set a few of the best aside for the top. Sprinkle the rest with the caster sugar and leave for 15 minutes, until they release some juice.
Whip: Whip the cold cream with the icing sugar and vanilla sugar to soft peaks. Don't overwhip it: it should only just hold its shape.
Fold: Fold the sugared berries and their juice gently into the cream with a spatula, in a few strokes, so the berries stay whole.
Serve: Spoon into glasses or bowls, top with the reserved berries and serve cold, with krumkake or biscuits. In Norway it is a Christmas dessert.

Respect local picking rules. In Nordland, Troms and Finnmark in northern Norway, landowners can ban cloudberry picking on their land, so look out for signs (eating berries on the spot is always allowed).

huckleberry-pie.title: Montana Huckleberry Pie
ingredients: 700 g huckleberries, fresh or frozen (no need to thaw)
150 g sugar, plus 1 tablespoon to sprinkle
instructions: Make the pastry: Rub the butter into the flour and salt until it looks like coarse crumbs with a few pea-sized lumps of butter. Add the iced water a spoonful at a time and bring it together into a dough. Divide it in two, flatten into discs, wrap and chill for at least 30 minutes.
Fill: Heat the oven to 220 °C. Roll out one disc and line a 23 cm pie dish with it. Mix the huckleberries with the sugar, cornflour and lemon juice and tip them into the pastry case.
Cover: Roll out the second disc, lay it over the filling, then trim and crimp the edges to seal. Cut a few slits in the top, brush with the egg and sprinkle with the extra sugar.

Bake: Bake for 20 minutes, then lower the oven to 180 °C and bake for another 40 minutes, until the crust is deep golden and thick juice bubbles through the slits. Put a tray underneath to catch any drips.
Cool: Leave the pie to cool for at least 3 hours, so the filling sets before you slice it. Serve with vanilla ice cream or whipped cream.

safetyNotes: Huckleberries are blue-black to purple, with a small crown at the tip like a blueberry. Don't eat red or white berries in clusters (baneberry is poisonous) or any berry you're not sure of.
Huckleberry patches are bear country: make noise and carry bear spray.

pawpaw-ice-cream.title: No-Churn Pawpaw Ice Cream
ingredients: 400 g ripe pawpaw pulp (from about 4–6 fruits)
instructions: Prepare the pulp: Halve the ripe pawpaws and scoop out the flesh with a spoon, leaving the skin behind. Pick out every seed by hand: not one should go into the blender.
Blend: Blend the pulp with the lime juice, condensed milk, salt and vanilla until smooth. The lime keeps the colour bright.
Whip: In a large bowl, whip the cream to soft peaks.
Fold: Fold the pawpaw mixture into the cream in two or three batches, until no streaks remain. Pour into a loaf tin or a freezer box.
Freeze: Cover and freeze for at least 6 hours, or overnight. Let it soften for 10 minutes before scooping.

Some people react to pawpaw with a stomach upset or a skin rash, so try a little first.

rose-hip-syrup.title: Rose Hip Syrup
ingredients: A jelly bag or fine cloth, and sterilised bottles
instructions: Prepare: Wash the hips, pull off the stalks and the dry tips, and chop them roughly in a food processor or with a knife.

First infusion: Bring 2 litres of the water to the boil, add the hips and bring back to the boil, then take off the heat and leave for 15 minutes. Pour into a scalded jelly bag or fine cloth and let the juice drip through.

Second infusion: Put the pulp back in the pan with the remaining litre of water, bring to the boil, leave for 10 minutes and strain again. Then pour all the juice through a clean, fine cloth once more, to catch every last hair.
Reduce: Boil the juice until it has reduced to about 1 litre. Add the sugar and lemon juice, stir until the sugar dissolves and boil for 5 minutes.
Bottle: Pour the hot syrup into hot sterilised bottles and seal them. Once opened, keep in the fridge and use within 2 weeks. Pour it over pancakes or ice cream, or dilute it with water for a drink.

Pick hips that are deep red and slightly soft, after the first frosts if you can. Don't pick beside busy roads.

sloe-jelly.title: Sloe and Apple Jelly
ingredients: 1 kg cooking apples, such as Bramley
Sugar: 750 g for each litre of juice
A jelly bag and sterilised jars
instructions: Prepare: Rinse the sloes and pick off any stalks and leaves. Chop the apples roughly without peeling or coring them: the peel and cores hold the pectin that sets the jelly.

Simmer: Put the sloes and apples in a large pan with just enough water to cover them. Simmer gently for about 45 minutes, stirring now and then, until the fruit is very soft. Press the apples lightly with a spoon, but don't mash the sloes, so the stones stay whole.
Strain: Tip everything into a scalded jelly bag set over a bowl and let it drip for several hours or overnight. Don't squeeze the bag, or the jelly will be cloudy.

Boil: Measure the juice into a clean pan and add 750 g of sugar for every litre. Stir over a low heat until the sugar dissolves, then boil hard for 10–15 minutes, until it reaches setting point: 105 °C, or a drop on a cold plate wrinkles when you push it.
Pot: Skim off any foam, pour into hot sterilised jars and seal. Serve with roast lamb, game or cheese.

Look-alikes are poisonous: deadly nightshade has shiny black berries sitting on a green star, on a soft, non-woody plant; buckthorn (Rhamnus cathartica) has shiny black berries in clusters and is strongly purgative.

sea-buckthorn-curd.title: Sea Buckthorn Curd
ingredients: About 300 g sea buckthorn berries, for 150 ml juice
instructions: Juice: Rinse the berries and press them through a fine sieve with the back of a spoon, to get about 150 ml of juice. Throw away the skins and seeds.
Mix: In a heatproof bowl, whisk the eggs, egg yolk, sugar and salt, then whisk in the juice.

Cook: Set the bowl over a pan of barely simmering water, without letting it touch the water. Stir all the time for 10–12 minutes, until the curd is thick enough to coat the back of a spoon (about 80 °C). Don't let it boil.
Finish: Take the bowl off the heat and stir in the butter a few pieces at a time, until smooth. For a silky curd, pass it through a sieve.
Store: Pour into warm sterilised jars, cover and leave to cool. Keep in the fridge and eat within 2 weeks. Spread it on toast or scones, or use it to fill tarts.

safetyNotes: Pick bright orange, juicy berries from late summer on, by hand or into a bowl. Don't break or cut branches off wild shrubs: it damages them, and in Finland it is forbidden.
Picking may be forbidden in protected dunes and nature reserves, so check local rules. The shrub is very thorny: wear gloves.

chicken-of-the-woods-piccata.title: Chicken of the Woods Piccata
ingredients: 400 g young chicken of the woods, the tender outer edges
instructions: Trim: Use only the soft outer 5–10 cm of young brackets and cut away anything tough or woody. Brush them clean and slice them 1 cm thick.
Fry: Season the slices, dust them with flour and fry them in the oil over a medium-high heat for 4–5 minutes a side, until golden and cooked through. Set them aside.
Sauce: Melt the butter in the same pan and cook the garlic for 30 seconds. Add the stock, lemon juice and capers and simmer for 2 minutes.
Finish: Return the mushrooms to the pan, turn them in the sauce for a minute and scatter with parsley. Serve with rice, pasta or bread.

safetyNotes: Always cook chicken of the woods through: raw or undercooked, it upsets the stomach.
Some people react to it even when it is cooked. The first time, eat a small portion and wait a day.
Don't pick brackets growing on yew, eucalyptus or conifers, which are linked to more reactions, or old ones that have turned pale, crumbly or chalky.

garlic-oyster-mushroom-noodles.title: Garlic Oyster Mushroom Noodles
ingredients: 2 spring onions, sliced, white and green parts apart
instructions: Prepare: Tear the mushrooms into strips along the gills and cut off any tough stem bases. Cook the noodles as the packet says and drain them.
Sear: Heat the oil in a wide pan and lay the mushrooms in one layer. Fry them without stirring for 3–4 minutes, then turn them and cook 3 minutes more, until browned at the edges.
Season: Add the garlic and the white parts of the spring onions for 1 minute, then the soy sauce, sugar and sesame oil.
Toss: Add the noodles and toss until glossy and hot. Serve with the spring onion greens, sesame seeds and chilli.

Sear: Heat the oil in a wide pan and lay the mushrooms in one layer. Fry them without stirring for 3–4 minutes, then turn them and cook 3 minutes more, until browned at the edges.
Season: Add the garlic and the white parts of the spring onions for 1 minute, then the soy sauce, sugar and sesame oil.
Toss: Add the noodles and toss until glossy and hot. Serve with the spring onion greens, sesame seeds and chilli.

warnings: Do not consume wild mushrooms unless identified by an expert.
safetyNotes: Cook oyster mushrooms well and don't eat them raw.
Use young, firm specimens: old ones go tough and often hide beetle larvae.
Don't confuse them with angel's wings (Pleurocybella porrigens), which is toxic: thin, pure white and growing on conifer wood.

elderflower-cordial.title: Elderflower Cordial
ingredients: 25 g citric acid (optional, helps it keep)
instructions: Pick: Pick creamy, fully open heads on a dry, sunny morning, away from busy roads. Shake out any insects, but don't wash them: the scent is in the pollen.
Syrup: Bring the water and sugar to the boil, stirring until the sugar has dissolved, then leave it to cool until lukewarm.
Steep: Add the flowers, lemon slices and citric acid, cover and leave in a cool place for 24–48 hours, stirring once a day.
Bottle: Strain through a sieve lined with muslin into sterilised bottles and seal. Keep in the fridge for up to 6 weeks, or freeze it. Dilute about 1 to 10 with still or sparkling water.

Elder is a woody shrub or small tree. Don't use dwarf elder (Sambucus ebulus), a non-woody plant with toxic parts, or the ground-growing white umbels of poisonous plants such as hemlock.

elderberry-syrup.title: Spiced Elderberry Syrup
ingredients: 500 g ripe elderberries, stripped from the stalks
instructions: Strip: Use only fully ripe, black berries. Strip them from the stalks with a fork and throw away any green berries and every bit of stalk.
Simmer: Put the berries, water and spices in a pan, bring to the boil and simmer gently for 20 minutes.
Strain: Mash the berries lightly and strain the juice through a fine sieve or muslin, pressing gently.

Sweeten: Return the juice to the pan with the lemon juice and sugar and simmer for 5 minutes, until the sugar has dissolved. If you use honey, stir it in off the heat once the juice is lukewarm. Bottle and keep in the fridge for up to 3 months. A spoonful in hot water makes a winter drink.

Use only black elder (Sambucus nigra) or American elder (S. canadensis), shrubs with flat clusters of berries. Red elder (S. racemosa) and dwarf elder (S. ebulus) are not used.

blackberry-apple-crumble.title: Blackberry and Apple Crumble
instructions: Fruit: Heat the oven to 190 °C. Toss the blackberries and apples with the sugar and lemon juice and spread them in a baking dish.
Crumble: Rub the butter into the flour with your fingertips until it looks like breadcrumbs, then stir in the brown sugar, oats and salt.
Top: Scatter the crumble loosely over the fruit without pressing it down.
Bake: Bake for 35–40 minutes, until golden on top and bubbling at the edges. Leave it to rest for 10 minutes and serve with cream, custard or ice cream.

safetyNotes: Pick above knee height and away from busy roads and sprayed field edges.
Rinse the berries just before using them and check them for small insects and mould.

wild-blueberry-pancakes.title: Wild Blueberry Pancakes
ingredients: 30 g butter, melted, plus butter for the pan
Maple syrup or honey to serve
instructions: Batter: Whisk the flour, baking powder, sugar and salt. Whisk the eggs, milk and melted butter separately and stir them in until just combined: a few lumps are fine.
Fry: Melt a little butter in a frying pan over a medium heat. Pour in small ladles of batter and scatter blueberries over each.
Turn: When bubbles appear and the edges set, after about 2 minutes, turn the pancakes and cook them for 1–2 minutes more.
Serve: Stack them warm with the rest of the berries and the syrup.

Turn: When bubbles appear and the edges set, after about 2 minutes, turn the pancakes and cook them for 1–2 minutes more.
Serve: Stack them warm with the rest of the berries and the syrup.

safetyNotes: In much of Europe low-growing berries can carry eggs of the fox tapeworm (Echinococcus multilocularis). Wash them well. Cooking kills the eggs, freezing doesn't, so cooked berries are the safer choice there.
Bilberries and blueberries grow on low shrubs. Deadly nightshade, which is very poisonous, has single shiny black berries sitting on a green star, on a tall soft plant.

hazelnut-cocoa-spread.title: Homemade Hazelnut Cocoa Spread
ingredients: 60 g icing sugar or maple syrup
instructions: Roast: Roast the hazelnuts at 180 °C for 10–12 minutes, until fragrant and the skins crack.
Skin: Rub the warm nuts in a clean tea towel to take off most of the skins.
Grind: Blend the nuts in a food processor for 5–10 minutes, scraping down the sides now and then, until they turn into a runny butter.
Flavour: Add the cocoa, sugar, chocolate, salt and vanilla and blend again, adding the oil a spoonful at a time until smooth and spreadable. Keep it in a clean jar in the fridge for up to 3 weeks.

Gather only nuts that have ripened and fallen in late summer and autumn. Throw away nuts with holes, which weevils have bored, and any that taste mouldy or bitter.

wild-mint-pea-soup.title: Pea Soup with Wild Mint
ingredients: A large handful of wild mint leaves (about 15 g), plus a few small ones to garnish
Salt, pepper and a squeeze of lemon
instructions: Soften: Cook the onion gently in the butter for 5 minutes, then add the potato and the stock and simmer for 10 minutes.
Peas: Add the peas and simmer for 3–4 minutes, just until tender, so they stay bright green.
Blend: Take the pan off the heat, add the mint leaves and blend until smooth. Season with salt, pepper and lemon.
Serve: Swirl in the cream and scatter with the small mint leaves. It is good hot or chilled.

safetyNotes: A wild mint smells clearly of mint when you crush a leaf: no mint smell, no mint.
Leave out pennyroyal (Mentha pulegium: small, rounded leaves, creeping stems, flowers in rings up the stem). It is toxic in larger amounts and must be avoided in pregnancy.
Pick water mint from clean streams, not from wet pasture grazed by sheep or cattle, where it can carry liver fluke.

candied-violets.title: Candied Sweet Violets
ingredients: 30–40 sweet violet flowers with a short stem
1 very fresh egg white, pasteurised if you can get it
instructions: Pick: Pick freshly opened flowers on a dry day and leave a short stem to hold them by. Check them for insects.
Paint: Beat the egg white lightly until just frothy. Holding a flower by its stem, paint every petal, front and back, with a thin layer.
Sugar: Sprinkle the flower all over with caster sugar, shake off the excess and set it face up on baking paper.

Dry: Leave them in a warm, dry place for 1–2 days, until completely crisp, then snip off the stems. Store them in an airtight tin between layers of paper for a few weeks and use them on cakes and desserts.

safetyNotes: Use only sweet violets (Viola odorata) or other wild violets. African violets (Saintpaulia) are not related and should not be eaten.
Raw egg white carries a small risk of salmonella: use pasteurised egg white for small children, pregnant people and the elderly.
Pick where no herbicides are sprayed and away from paths used by dogs.

plantain-leaf-crisps.title: Plantain Leaf Crisps
ingredients: 2 large handfuls of young plantain leaves
instructions: Heat: Heat the oven to 150 °C (130 °C fan).
Prepare: Pick young, tender leaves no bigger than your palm. Wash them and dry them completely: any water left steams them instead of crisping them.
Season: Toss the leaves with the oil and seasonings so each is lightly coated, then lay them flat on baking paper without overlapping.
Bake: Bake for 15–20 minutes, turning them once, until crisp but still green. Let them cool on the tray and eat them the same day.

safetyNotes: Pick away from roadsides, dog-walking paths and sprayed lawns: plantain likes trampled ground.
Plantain leaves have strong parallel veins that pull out like strings. Foxglove leaves, which are poisonous, have a network of veins and are softly hairy.

pickled-daisy-buds.title: Pickled Daisy Buds
instructions: Pick: Pick tight green buds, before any white shows, from clean lawns and meadows. Rinse and drain them.
Salt: Toss the buds with the salt and leave them for 12 hours to draw out the moisture, then rinse them and pat them dry.
Brine: Bring the vinegar, water, sugar, bay leaf and peppercorns to the boil.
Jar: Pack the buds and the dill into the jar, pour the hot vinegar over to cover them and seal. Leave for at least 2 weeks before eating. Use them like capers in salads, sauces and with fish.

Pick from lawns that are not sprayed or fertilised, away from areas used by dogs.
People allergic to the daisy family (Asteraceae), for example to ragweed or chamomile, can react to them.
